result: AAV–mDlx5/6–ChR2–mCherry selectively transduces GABAergic neurons in macaque V1, with particularly high efficiency for parvalbumin-positive neurons. Histological analysis showed that 468/543 (86%) of mCherry-positive neurons co-expressed parvalbumin, significantly higher than expected by chance (p<0.005), and mCherry-positive cells exhibited non-pyramidal morphologies consistent with GABAergic identity.
evaluation: Claims C2-C5 provide converging histological evidence for selective GABAergic transduction. The quantitative co-localization data (C3, C5) with statistical validation, morphological observations (C2), and appropriate citation of prior work (C1, C4) collectively support the conclusion. The binomial test appropriately assesses whether parvalbumin co-expression exceeds chance expectations.

result: Optical stimulation modulates neural activity at recording sites in V1, with 38/56 sites showing increased spiking and short-latency responses (<5 ms at 11 sites, mean 14±26 ms) consistent with direct ChR2 activation of GABAergic neurons that subsequently suppress other neurons via synaptic inhibition.
evaluation: Claims C6-C9 provide quantitative electrophysiological data demonstrating optical modulation of neural activity with appropriate temporal characteristics. The short latencies at some sites (C9) support the inference (C10) that directly activated ChR2-expressing neurons mediate suppression of other neurons, though C10 remains inferential rather than directly demonstrated.

result: Optogenetic stimulation using AAV–mDlx5/6–ChR2 does not produce rebound activity following laser termination, unlike halorhodopsin-based approaches. Post-laser firing rates exceeded pre-laser rates at only 2/18 suppressed sites, with recovery times ranging from 0-215 ms (median 97.5 ms).
evaluation: Claims C11-C14 provide appropriate comparison with prior methods (C11) and quantitative evidence (C13, C14) that rebound activity is rare with this approach (C12). The data support a key advantage of the ChR2-based inhibitory neuron stimulation method over direct hyperpolarization approaches.

result: Optical stimulation impairs visually guided saccades in a retinotopically specific manner. Monkeys failed to make saccades into the receptive fields of stimulated neurons on laser trials, with saccade endpoints farther from targets (p<0.002 for monkey 2, p=0.03 for monkey 3) and longer latencies (p<0.0001 for both monkeys) when targets appeared inside the RFs, but not when targets appeared elsewhere.
evaluation: Claims C15-C18 provide converging behavioral evidence with appropriate statistical tests demonstrating spatial specificity of the optogenetic effect. The retinotopic specificity (C16) and quantitative comparisons with statistical validation (C17, C18) strongly support the conclusion that optical stimulation produces localized behavioral deficits.

result: Optical stimulation profoundly impairs contrast detection performance. Both monkeys detected visual stimuli more frequently on control than laser trials (p<0.001), with neither monkey achieving above-chance accuracy on laser trials even at maximum contrast. In most sessions (10/11 for monkey 2, 11/12 for monkey 3) and blocks (52/69 and 63/81 respectively), optical stimulation significantly reduced detection or increased thresholds beyond display limits.
evaluation: Claims C19-C22 provide extensive quantitative behavioral data with appropriate statistical tests across multiple sessions and blocks. The consistency of effects across animals and the magnitude of impairment (inability to detect even maximum contrast stimuli, C20) strongly support the conclusion of profound behavioral effects.

result: The behavioral effects of optical stimulation are dose-dependent, stable over time, and do not show evidence of compensation. Effects increased steeply with laser power between 12.8-22.3 mW and saturated by 30.0 mW, remained consistent across ~1000 trials (~50 mins), showed no correlation with block number (r=0.18, p=0.59), and did not differ between early and late trials (p=0.79).
evaluation: Claims C23-C27 provide comprehensive characterization of the temporal stability and dose-response properties of the optogenetic manipulation. The statistical analyses appropriately test for adaptation or compensation effects, and the lack of such effects (C26, C27) distinguishes this approach from prior work. Control trial performance was unaffected by laser power (C24), supporting specificity.

result: Monkeys acquired subtle visual deficits in optogenetically manipulated regions, assessed 22 months post-experiment in monkey 2. The deficit is attributed to potential tissue damage from high laser power (4-160 mW), tissue heating (likely several °C), or repeated fiber penetrations, though consistency of acute behavioral effects argues against acute damage during experiments.
evaluation: Claims C39-C44 acknowledge long-term tissue effects but involve substantial speculation about causes (C41, C43). While C40 provides behavioral data showing subtle deficits, C42 documents higher laser power than other studies, and C44 argues against acute damage, the causal attribution remains uncertain. The lack of histological data from monkey 2 and the confound of prior single-unit recordings (C41) limit definitive conclusions.

result: The threshold changes observed in this study (~>100%) were substantially larger than those in previous optogenetic inactivation studies (~5%), potentially due to multiple factors including selective activation of inhibitory neurons, use of ChR2 (higher ion conductance than pumps), higher laser power, and targeting V1 which is indispensable for the tested behaviors.
evaluation: Claims C49-C50 provide appropriate comparison with prior work and offer plausible mechanistic explanations supported by citations. While C50 involves some speculation, the proposed mechanisms are well-grounded in established principles (ion channel vs pump efficiency, inhibitory neuron connectivity, area-specific necessity) and supported by relevant citations.

result: The optogenetic manipulation produced changes in visual sensitivity rather than criterion alone, as assessed by signal detection theory. The brevity and unpredictability of optical stimulation makes large, consistent criterion changes on laser trials unlikely.
evaluation: Claims C53-C54 appropriately address the sensitivity vs. criterion distinction using signal detection theory framework. The argument that brief, unpredictable stimulation is unlikely to produce strategic criterion shifts (C54) is reasonable, though the analysis would be strengthened by explicit presentation of criterion measures alongside d' values.

result: Unlike prior work using non-selective promoters that produced phosphenes, selective stimulation of inhibitory neurons with AAV–mDlx5/6–ChR2 did not cause monkeys to make saccades into stimulated receptive fields, suggesting no phosphene perception. This difference is attributed to the neuronal population stimulated (inhibitory vs. mixed excitatory/inhibitory).
evaluation: Claims C34-C37 provide appropriate comparison with prior work (Jazayeri et al., 2012) and identify the key methodological difference (promoter selectivity). The behavioral observations (C35) support the inference of no phosphene, and the attribution to neuronal population differences (C36, C37) is well-reasoned. C38 offers a testable hypothesis for future work.

result: Tissue damage from optogenetic manipulations can be mitigated through technical improvements including artificial dura (reducing mechanical damage), red-shifted opsins (reducing thermal damage from lower tissue heating), and step-function opsins (allowing brief, safe pulses to produce sustained effects).
evaluation: Claims C45-C48 provide well-supported recommendations for future work, appropriately citing prior studies (C45, C48) and explaining the mechanistic basis for each improvement (C46-C48). These represent established approaches in the field rather than speculative proposals.

result: Optogenetic phototagging using AAV–mDlx5/6–ChR2 enables decisive electrophysiological identification of inhibitory neurons in macaques, addressing the challenge that fast-spiking excitatory neurons in primates undermine traditional spike waveform-based classification methods.
evaluation: Claims C55-C58 appropriately cite prior work on cell-type differences (C55) and classification challenges (C57), identify the technical problem (C56), and demonstrate the solution with data (C58, Figure 9). This represents an important methodological contribution beyond the primary inactivation results.

result: Optogenetic stimulation of inhibitory neurons using AAV–mDlx5/6–ChR2 is a powerful method for spatiotemporally precise neural inactivation in macaques. The approach modulated spiking activity, profoundly reduced visual sensitivity in the represented region of space, avoided rebound firing, and maintained efficacy across >1000 trials.
evaluation: Claims C59-C63 represent the main conclusions of the study, appropriately synthesizing the major findings from histology (selectivity), electrophysiology (C61), behavior (C62), temporal properties (C63), and comparison with alternative methods. The conclusions are well-supported by the collective evidence presented throughout the manuscript.

result: Optogenetics provides the fastest reversible neural inactivation method currently available. While successful in rodents and used in pioneering macaque studies, prior approaches using direct hyperpolarization produced small behavioral effects, potentially due to counteracting suppression of inhibitory neurons. An alternative approach activating inhibitory neurons with ChR2 has advantages including higher ion conductance and leveraging GABAergic connectivity.
evaluation: Claims C28-C33 provide appropriate context from prior work, accurately citing studies in rodents (C29, C32) and macaques (C30), and identifying limitations of previous approaches (C31). The rationale for the ChR2-based inhibitory neuron approach (C33) is well-grounded in established principles and appropriately cited.

result: The study used three male rhesus monkeys (7-14 kg), with two implanted for chronic recordings. AAV injections targeted V1 with different serotypes and volumes (AAV9 in monkey 2, AAV1 in monkey 3), followed by histological analysis in monkey 1 (45 days post-injection) and electrophysiological recordings in monkeys 2-3 (3-4 weeks post-injection). Recording sites were selected based on visual responsiveness and audible firing rate changes during optical stimulation.
evaluation: Claims C64-C71 provide standard methodological details about subjects, surgical procedures, injection parameters, and site selection criteria. These are appropriately documented and support reproducibility, though the site selection criterion (C71, audible change) introduces potential bias toward strongly modulated sites.

result: Behavioral performance was analyzed using signal detection theory (d' calculated from hit and false alarm rates), psychometric functions were fit with Weibull distributions using maximum likelihood with binomial error, and detection threshold was defined as 82% correct performance.
evaluation: Claims C72-C74 describe standard, well-established analysis methods appropriately cited (C72). The Weibull fitting procedure (C73) and threshold definition (C74) are conventional approaches for psychophysical data analysis.
